Shipping each order from China can be attractive for a small brand because eligible Section 321 shipments valued at no more than $800 have historically entered duty- and tax-free, reducing landed cost and avoiding the cash tied up in US inventory. [shard_04647_72515]

That advantage is not the same as “anything under $800 is exempt,” because each parcel still needs an accurate commercial invoice, country of origin, HS code, description, quantity, weight, value, and any required permits. [shard_05461_22280]

I could not establish from the available evidence whether the $800 China-to-US treatment remains unchanged on 23 July 2026, so you should obtain a current written ruling or broker confirmation before changing your supply chain.

The policy risk is material because the US threshold has drawn proposals for tighter restrictions, partly because the US threshold is far higher than China’s cited threshold and because lawmakers argue that the arrangement disadvantages domestic businesses. [shard_01256_1845]

A direct-to-consumer model also makes your brand dependent on air-parcel economics rather than ocean freight and domestic fulfillment, with ordinary air freight described as roughly 6–13 days and express service as roughly 1–4 days before exceptions, customs holds, or last-mile variation. [shard_05461_22280]

Those shipping costs, per-order pick-and-pack fees, returns, lost parcels, customer-service work, and the need to replace defective items can consume much of the nominal tariff saving, especially for low-priced or bulky products.

The biggest compliance danger is not merely a delayed parcel but an excluded shipment, customer harm, or reputational damage if your supplier cannot prove origin and labor conditions through the full supply chain.

The UFLPA presumption covers goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang and goods connected to designated entities, including some entities outside Xinjiang, so routing a product through another country does not cleanse its origin or labor risk. [shard_04073_1206]

Direct shipment also attracts the same scrutiny that has surrounded Shein and Temu, whose sub-$800 parcel models have been criticized as reducing visibility into manufacturing and trade practices. [shard_00617_39888]

Before using the model, require supplier-level bills of materials, factory identities, country-of-origin records, labor attestations, transaction records, test reports, and an indemnity that is backed by a financially credible counterparty, and audit a sample rather than accepting a generic “compliant” certificate.

For a small brand, the sensible default is usually a hybrid pilot: direct-ship only lightweight, low-return, low-regulation products with reliable suppliers, while holding proven best sellers in a US third-party warehouse for predictable delivery and returns.

US inventory costs more upfront and exposes you to duty and carrying-cost risk, but it buys control over delivery promises, customer experience, inspection, bundling, and returns, which are often more valuable to a brand than the last few points of import savings.

A Mexico-based model can combine Chinese sourcing with a bonded-warehouse and cross-border parcel workflow, and the evidence describes that structure as a way to ship orders into the US while seeking Section 321 treatment. [shard_04647_72515]

Mexico is therefore a useful regional-fulfillment option when your customers are concentrated in the US and you can manage Mexican warehousing, customs status, origin documentation, broker liability, and the possibility that a future US rule change removes the intended benefit.

Canada may be attractive for northern-US or Canadian demand, while Mexico is generally the more natural test for US proximity, but neither location automatically converts Chinese goods into North American goods or eliminates US customs and forced-labor obligations.

The available North American trade evidence points to lower delivery costs, more standardized customs procedures, and easier cross-border commerce under CUSMA, but those benefits should be modeled product by product rather than treated as a blanket exemption. [shard_03218_73710]

Use a landed-cost spreadsheet containing product cost, China-to-fulfillment freight, parcel postage, duties and fees under both eligible and ineligible scenarios, warehouse and pick fees, returns, chargebacks, inspection, compliance, and an assumed policy-change contingency.

My recommendation is not to make direct China-to-customer shipping your entire supply chain: test it narrowly, maintain a US-stocked fallback for core products, and move toward US or regional inventory when delivery reliability, repeat purchases, returns, or compliance exposure matter more than the nominal Section 321 saving.
